title-group.article-title: WHO Target Product Profiles for Dengue Therapeutics: An Interdisciplinary Analysis of Ethical, Regulatory, and Implementation Considerations

abstract.p: Dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, is experiencing its largest surge in history, driven by climate and demographic change. Expanding transmission has highlighted previously under-recognised populations at heightened risk of severe disease, including people with multimorbidity and immunosuppression, for whom live-attenuated vaccines are contraindicated or unlicensed. This evolving epidemiology underscores the urgent need for safe and effective treatments for dengue, particularly for those with complex risk profiles compounded by socio-economic disadvantage. We examine ethical, regulatory, and implementation considerations to support World Health Organization target product profile development for dengue therapeutics. Our analysis highlights the need for better characterisation of risk groups, including through enhanced surveillance; co-produced approaches for their inclusion in research prioritisation, trials, and care; and strategies to address key barriers to access for all, such as rapid diagnostics. This framework has the potential to inform equitable development and delivery of countermeasures for other infectious threats to global health.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Dengue is the most important mosquito-borne viral disease of humans and is experiencing its largest surge in history1,2. Following a tenfold increase in reported cases over the past two decades, 2024 was the worst year for dengue on record1,2. On 1 December 2023, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared dengue a Grade 3 global health emergency and, in October 2024, launched a cross-departmental global preparedness and response plan1.

This health emergency is the consequence of forces favouring the spread of the vector and virus, together with the unprecedented rise in numbers of people at risk of developing severe3—and potentially fatal—disease. Climate change4,5, globalisation6 (including travel), and urbanisation7 have extended transmission seasons and expanded the range of Aedes mosquito vectors beyond Asia and Latin America, into Europe8,9, North America10, and Africa11. In parallel, rapidly ageing populations12 and the rising prevalence of (often undiagnosed) diabetes mellitus13 and other features of the metabolic syndrome—particularly in increasingly affluent Asia and Latin America13—have created large populations at heightened risk of complications and poorer outcomes from dengue infection12,14. These risks are compounded by immune dysfunction associated with immunosenescence and chronic inflammation. Higher co-circulation of multiple dengue virus serotypes further increases the likelihood and frequency of severe secondary heterotypic infections15.

Vector control has long been the cornerstone of dengue prevention1. These population-level approaches include eliminating mosquito breeding areas and more recently, introducing Wolbachia bacteria into local Aedes populations to reduce vector competency16. In addition to vector control, a pan-serotype live-attenuated dengue vaccine (Qdenga®17) is now licensed in multiple countries and conditionally recommended by WHO for routine use in areas of high transmission intensity for children aged 6-16 years18, with another live-attenuated vaccine recently completing phase 3 clinical trials19. However, these approaches face substantial challenges: extreme weather events and unplanned migration are overwhelming vector control20 and health systems1, while live-attenuated vaccines are contraindicated18, unlicensed, or lack efficacy data in groups at increased risk of severe dengue outcomes, including pregnant and lactating women21,22 and immunosuppressed populations23.

No pathogen-specific drugs for dengue are available to date and supportive care, if accessible, remains the mainstay of clinical management24. The expanding geographic distribution and complexity of dengue risk underscores the need for therapeutics to reduce progression to severe disease, particularly those for whom vaccines25,26 and supportive care alone may be insufficient in resource-limited or outbreak settings. Populations at increased risk of severe disease, once a minority of cases, have now increased significantly in absolute numbers. This reflects the exponential growth in the overall incidence of dengue cases12,27, further straining already overstretched health systems.

WHO target product profiles (TPPs) for treatments for dengue were developed as part of the WHO response to the Grade 3 global dengue emergency. They serve as a strategic reference for product developers, regulatory agencies, procurement bodies, and funders (Figure 1) to facilitate alignment between public health and R&D priorities ahead of phase 3 trials28. WHO TPPs define minimally acceptable (essential) and preferred (optimal) product criteria, specifying the intended use, target populations, and desired product characteristics, prioritising access and affordability considerations throughout development28. TPPs therefore make explicit many of the normative choices embedded in therapeutics development, including decisions about which populations should be prioritised, what levels of benefit justify potential risks, and how products should be designed to enable equitable access. The dengue therapeutics clinical development pipeline, together with the scientific and operational aspects underpinning the TPPs, is described in our companion article29. In this article, we examine ethical, regulatory, and implementation considerations arising across key domains of the WHO dengue therapeutics TPPs (Table 1)—including indication for use, target populations, safety and efficacy assessment, and access considerations—to inform development of these TPPs. For each domain, we highlight ethical challenges that arise from the specific epidemiology and clinical features of dengue along with their implications for research, development, and implementation. Table 1 links WHO TPP domains to these associated considerations as an integrated framework. Our analysis draws on widely recognised principles in global health ethics—including equity, justice, stakeholder engagement, and trustworthiness—and considers how these principles apply to WHO dengue therapeutics TPP development during a global emergency.

sec.title: Expert Development Group: Inclusive Representation and Engagement for Priority Setting for Global Health
sec.p: The initiation of the WHO TPP development process establishes research and development for dengue therapeutics as a global health priority28. Dengue has historically received limited investment in drug development compared with its global disease burden, as evidenced by the absence of dengue-specific licensed treatments to date and a limited late-stage clinical development pipeline29. Greater prioritisation of dengue therapeutics research may therefore help address longstanding gaps in innovation for diseases that disproportionately affect populations in resource-limited settings. In allocating resources, non-commercial funders may consider supporting research likely to achieve sustainable and equitable reductions in dengue-related morbidity, mortality, and health system burden, particularly where commercial incentives for product development are limited30.

This prioritisation function is operationalised through the formation of a WHO TPP expert development group28, which serves as a key mechanism for translating global health priorities into product development specifications. Such a group28 for treatments for dengue should include representatives from all six WHO regions now affected by dengue, with diverse gender representation and experience caring for dengue patients across the life course and disease severities, as well as expertise spanning drug discovery, development, regulation, and access. This ensures the breadth and depth of expertise for authoritative global consensus on TPP specifications and priority setting for dengue drug development.

In keeping with the ‘all affected principle’, this expert group would ideally be informed by patient consultation and engagement31,32, particularly involving populations at increased risk of more severe dengue outcomes such as the elderly12, people with diabetes mellitus14 and related comorbidities, pregnant and lactating women22, and people with or on immunosuppression23. Including these groups is a matter of conducting just and fair procedures, hearing all relevant voices to reflect diverse lived experiences of dengue risk, barriers to care, and unmet therapeutic needs. Such engagement strengthens the legitimacy, fairness, and relevance of TPP-informed research prioritisation and product design. Capacity for such consultation mechanisms could be consistently strengthened between outbreaks to facilitate timely engagement in fluid emergency environments33.

sec.title: Indication for Use: Disease Stage Use Cases and Health System Requirements for Equitable Delivery
sec.p: The indication for use of a drug is the medical condition and circumstances under which it is licensed for use28. This could include whether the drug is for prevention or treatment, the stage or severity of the disease to be treated, and whether the treatment is the first choice (first-line) or should be given only after the first-line treatment has not worked (second-line).

Dengue is a multiphase disease. Non-specific symptoms of fever, headache, myalgia, and rash accompany brief viraemia of several days in early ‘febrile’ disease34. Most people recover from early dengue in the community without further complications. In some cases, there is progression to increasing capillary leakage due to an inflammatory host response characterised by shock, bleeding, and organ impairment in late ‘critical’ severe disease34. Healthcare costs per patient are highest in the critical phase when hospitalisation and organ support may be required34. The development of therapeutic approaches to reduce disease severity and prevent complications has been prioritised by WHO1, and prophylaxis (e.g. of household members post-exposure) may become of interest as longer-acting agents become available.

It can be challenging to differentiate early dengue from other co-circulating acute febrile illnesses and to determine when progression from early to late dengue disease is likely to occur35,36. Moreover, in keeping with other acute viral infections, the therapeutic time window for maximal effect of an antiviral for treatment of early dengue is likely to be brief (e.g. within 72 hours) following symptom onset meaning that rapid diagnosis within hours of presentation is likely to be essential for antivirals to be administered both for the correct indication and in time to be effective37. Increasing access to point-of-care and rapid virological diagnostic tests38 will therefore be central to the effective and equitable delivery of a dengue antiviral drug39. The growing number of health systems now battling dengue outbreaks1 presents a further challenge of developing drugs which can be adopted into policy and practice in the diverse health systems and levels of resourcing where they are most needed.

Given dengue’s non-specific presentation and the likely narrow time window for antivirals, use case analyses of the real-world health and dengue control systems in which a dengue antiviral would be utilised are vital to understand requirements for ethical delivery and meaningful health impact. In addition to mapping the patient pathway and the key processes feeding into decision-making for administration of medical interventions, this should include assessment of diagnostic capacity for detecting the virus and its related complications (such as thrombocytopenia), and assessment of the predictive value of the widely-used warning signs and biomarkers for detection of severe dengue36. Factors contributing to timing of presentation and other health-seeking behaviour would also be of importance40. These considerations highlight the need to strengthen health systems to support early linkage to care for all dengue patients, particularly in settings where resources are already strained by recent pandemics and recurrent outbreaks.

sec.title: Target Population: Vulnerable Groups, Geographic and Socioeconomic Inequities, and Global Health Justice
sec.p: The TPP target population refers to the patients among whom a drug should be used28. WHO further recommends inclusion of evidence requirements for vulnerable groups (e.g. young children41, pregnant and lactating women42, the elderly, and the immunosuppressed)28 who are typically excluded from or under-represented in pivotal trials43. In the case of dengue, an antiviral would be an important additional tool to complement vaccination in individuals predisposed to more severe and potentially fatal complications of infection. These include groups often under-represented in research43, for whom currently licensed dengue vaccines are contraindicated44 or potentially less efficacious, as well as those with additional comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus14 and other features of the metabolic syndrome or pre-existing organ failure15.

As global warming extends the range and transmission seasons of dengue’s Aedes mosquito vector, another important and evolving dimension of dengue risk, alongside demographic characteristics and comorbidities, is geography. There has been recent autochthonous dengue transmission in new locations in high-income Europe45,46 (e.g. France47) and North America46 (e.g. United States46), as well as outbreaks in all income settings in Africa11,46 (e.g. Burkina Faso48) with record numbers of deaths reported. Many populations in newly affected regions lack pre-existing immunity to dengue viruses and may have limited experience with dengue-specific vector control and surveillance systems. At the same time, extreme weather events and the resulting disruption of sanitation systems, such as waste management and piped water supply, have contributed to some of the deadliest dengue seasons in Latin America (e.g. Brazil) and Asia (e.g. Philippines) for decades1. Climate change in these emerging economies has disproportionately affected the rising numbers of internal migrants and those living in poverty in densely-populated urban areas, where dengue is one of a number of infections exacerbated by environmental disruption30,49. These trends highlight that dengue risk is increasingly shaped by intersecting geographic, climatic, socioeconomic, and health system vulnerabilities.

Populations historically most affected by dengue are likely to remain at greatest risk due to climate change, population growth, internal migration, and healthcare system stressors. Distribution of dengue therapeutics should therefore consider disease burden over time, including historical morbidity and mortality, alongside vulnerability to severe disease and health system capacity.

Accurate, ideally notification-based51, case reporting for assessments of dengue disease burden is therefore essential for equitable and effective allocation of resources52. Issues of global health justice arise if patterns of reporting align with patterns of advantage, such that even a few cases are recorded in well-resourced settings with effective surveillance platforms, yet many cases go unrecorded in less well-resourced settings52. This could lead to deprioritisation of settings where additional support in controlling the disease is needed most, resulting in worse overall health outcomes, and greater health inequities52. Continued strengthening and extension of notification-based surveillance systems in all income settings to include data collection on vulnerable groups, their clinical outcomes and health system resource utilisation with appropriate safeguards for patient privacy could further support targeting of dengue therapeutics delivery to areas of greatest need30,52.

Furthermore, clinical trials involving vulnerable groups typically under-represented in research should be incorporated into development planning from the outset, as well as across the spectrum of healthcare settings and health systems43. While early-phase trials are typically conducted in carefully selected populations to establish safety, subsequent studies should generate evidence to support the safe and effective use of dengue therapeutics in populations at greatest risk of severe disease. For dengue, this should also include individuals with comorbidities and pre-existing organ dysfunction. In addition, pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and formulation studies in these special populations should be conducted as early as possible in clinical development to support access to safe and effective medicines for these under-represented groups43,53. These efforts should be facilitated by continued strengthening of ethical review and regulatory expertise for medicines in these vulnerable populations, particularly in regions with the greatest disease burden43,54. Clinical management guidelines and pathways should in turn support these groups to access care3.

sec.title: Safety and Efficacy: Pan-serotype Performance, Validated Outcomes, and Trustworthiness across the Product Life Cycle
sec.p: Balancing safety and efficacy is central to the duty of care of the healthcare provider and system55,56, and is particularly complex in dengue where there is the theoretical risk of enhancement of disease by heterotypic antibodies. For example, there was significant public reaction to concerns about the possibility of vaccine-induced enhancement of disease in children seronegative at baseline who experienced higher rates of severe dengue and hospitalisation than their unvaccinated peers following the roll-out of a since-withdrawn dengue vaccine in the Philippines57. The controversy surrounding the vaccine was associated with reduced public confidence in vaccination programmes in subsequent years, underscoring the importance of fostering public trust at all stages of development and implementation of pharmacological interventions58,59. These experiences highlight how safety and efficacy considerations are closely linked to public trust and sustained health system legitimacy across the product life cycle. Trustworthiness is therefore both an instrumental and normative requirement of the development and delivery of therapeutics. It can be demonstrated by careful and appropriate balancing of considerations of health equity, non-health-related harms and benefits, and other factors alongside the safety and efficacy of a drug. One positive step is engaging populations receiving interventions through co-produced information and support to ensure that public health actions taken now will not undermine future efforts31,32.

From a normative and systems perspective, the acceptable level of toxicity of a drug should be proportional to the severity of the disease being shortened at the point of treatment and to that being averted if the disease had continued to become more complicated55,56. The evidence requirements for this would vary according to the frequency of the adverse effect and the likelihood of disease progression at both the population and individual levels. However, from a regulatory and post-marketing surveillance perspective, randomised controlled trials typically have safety outcomes as secondary endpoints and often exclude special populations, limiting their power and ability to fully capture adverse effects under real-world conditions of use43,60,61. Rare (<1 in 1000) adverse effects may only be detected in meta-analyses and post-marketing surveillance case reports55. For equitable access, given the broad range of populations and health systems now affected by dengue, as well as the very low overall population frequency of severe and fatal dengue, an antiviral drug for dengue treatment should be as safe as possible with no serious adverse effects and any adverse effects should ideally be detectable by routine pharmacovigilance without the need for additional monitoring (and the often resource-intensive specialist resources this would involve) in the general population62.

Importantly, a dengue medicine should not exacerbate the development of or be more likely to cause adverse effects in the presence of the cardinal dengue complications of vascular leak, bleeding, and organ failure (particularly liver63, kidneys, lungs, and central nervous system). Evaluation of potential safety issues relevant to vulnerable groups of young children (growth interactions), pregnant and lactating women (teratogenicity), the elderly and those with multiple comorbidities (drug and organ failure interactions), and those with or on immunosuppression (increased risk of opportunistic infections) should be considered as early as possible in development to enable these groups to access treatment43. Stakeholder consultation and patient engagement throughout development are also essential to define acceptable thresholds of risk, including for specific adverse effects and any additional monitoring requirements in special populations31. It should also be used to identify any unintended effects on patients’ lives which may not have otherwise been recognised by product developers (e.g. hair loss or the need to disclose infected status to employers) and may have resulted in reduced uptake and diminished trust in health authorities if not addressed31.

At the level of therapeutic modality, the two main drug modalities in clinical development for dengue (small molecules and monoclonal antibodies) differ in adverse effect profile, as summarised in Table 2. There is a theoretical concern about antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) of dengue disease from monoclonal antibody administration in individuals with pre-existing immunity to other dengue virus serotypes, potentially through fragment crystallisable region (Fc)-mediated mechanisms. Current candidates contain Fc-silencing mutations designed to disable Fc-mediated effector functions and mitigate ADE risk24. The high specificity of monoclonal antibodies means serious adverse drug reactions are otherwise rare and anti-infective monoclonal antibodies are generally considered safe in vulnerable groups64.

Given previous experience with dengue vaccines, careful causality assessment65,66 of adverse effects adjudicated by independent expert committees55 as well as transparent communication58 about any adverse effects observed in clinical trials and post-marketing use will be crucial to sustain trust in wide-scale use of a dengue medicine. Clarity in and harmonisation of choice and definitions of clinically relevant, feasible, acceptable, and validated outcomes for both safety and efficacy through core outcome set development67 are necessary to strengthen internal and external validity of findings55 as well as public trust in the scientific process. Together, these measures reinforce trustworthiness across the full product life cycle from early clinical development through to post-marketing surveillance.

High pan-serotype efficacy against all four serotypes of dengue virus in both primary and secondary dengue would be vital for a drug to be used in any geographic and resource setting as well as in outbreaks where serotype information is usually not available immediately if at all38. In vivo evidence from clinical trials would be preferable, as no animal models adequately recapitulate human disease, and controlled human infection models are now available for all four dengue virus serotypes, including DENV-3 and DENV-4 which have historically been uncommon in natural infection24. Dengue vaccine efficacy outcome thresholds (e.g. >80% efficacy against virologically-confirmed hospitalised dengue infection19) may provide instructive comparators.

At the same time, efficacy outcome measure selection and standardisation for dengue therapeutics have specific complexities. Viral load kinetics in early-phase trials of natural infection provide a direct measure of drug potency and a surrogate measure of drug efficacy, but vary also with dengue virus serotype and genotype as well as host demographics, previous infection status, and likely comorbidities68–70. Controlled human infection models standardise viral inoculum and strain as well as host characteristics for a cleaner read-out of antiviral potency, but viral challenge strains are selected to produce mild to moderate dengue illness so would not be suitable for evaluation of clinical outcomes related to progression to severe disease (including warning signs)24. Healthcare setting-based resource utilisation outcomes like primary care visits, intravenous fluid administration71, hospitalisation, or transfer to a critical care environment for organ support are relatively common but confounded by local resource availability and clinical practices, which may evolve over the course of even a single outbreak. Established clinical outcomes of severe dengue (vascular leak, bleeding, organ failure) and death are of clear public health relevance but are of low frequency in the general population1 and could require prohibitively large sample sizes for adequately powered clinical trials to detect a difference between treatment groups. This creates a tension between feasibility of trial design and clinical relevance of outcomes in the development of dengue therapeutics. Enrichment of randomised trials of dengue treatment with individuals at risk of more severe outcomes, or targeted trials of dengue risk groups alone, could be two approaches to obtain high-quality evidence in groups for whom live-attenuated vaccines may not be suitable and would be most in need of a dengue medicine to prevent progression to severe dengue72.

There is also interest in the development and validation of measures of recovery from acute signs (e.g. fever) and symptoms (e.g. pain) similar to symptom scores for acute respiratory infections. These are composite outcomes, which, while appealing for providing a semi-quantitative measurement of the patient experience, should be employed with caution because of the risk of misinterpretation55. Where composite outcomes are chosen in the absence of practical clinical alternatives (e.g. due to rarity of objective clinical outcomes), sufficient detail should be collected to allow analysis of individual components for appropriate clinical and public health prioritisation55.

There is currently limited information available about the risk of development of resistance in clinical use of current dengue drug candidates in late development. Experience from other acute viral infections suggests that escape mutations against monoclonal antibodies can emerge more rapidly than resistance to small molecule drugs64. The use of combination therapies such as those used in malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV would be an approach to reduce the likelihood of resistance emerging in clinical deployment.

sec.title: Dose Regimen: Balancing Regimen Design, Patient Experience, and Resource Availability for Equitable Access at Scale
sec.p: Dose regimen considerations include dose, route, formulation, frequency, and duration of administration28. This is determined by the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drug, which are evaluated through dedicated clinical studies to maximise safety and efficacy in target patient groups and body compartments, as discussed above.

The resources required of the patient and health system to access treatment should be appropriate relative to the duration of dengue illness shortened or averted by treatment. Dengue generally causes an acute febrile illness lasting around a week or less, approximately corresponding with viraemia, and the vast majority of people are managed in home or community settings34. Less invasive routes of administration with formulations that do not compromise bodily integrity (oral73 tablet forms, including dispersible formulations) and lower dose frequencies74 (once or twice daily) are associated with higher adherence and acceptability of drug regimens. The standard of care for uncomplicated malaria is a three-day treatment course of oral artemisinin-based combination therapy once or twice daily75. Similarly, uncomplicated urinary tract and lower respiratory tract infections, the most common bacterial infections causing acute febrile illness in adults, are typically treated with a three- (urinary tract) to five-day (lower respiratory tract) courses of oral antibiotics at a frequency ranging from twice to four times daily76. Oral formulations do not require additional equipment or specialised healthcare settings for administration, which would facilitate rapid scale-up in an outbreak or global emergency53. Currently, only small molecule candidates77,78 are available via the oral route while monoclonal antibody candidates79 are administered intravenously. However, half-life–extending mutations can prolong protection from monoclonal antibodies from days to months80.

There has been much debate about the narrow therapeutic time window for antiviral drugs in dengue37 in real-world settings. While early administration is necessary for an optimal read-out in pivotal trials, clinical decision-making is more nuanced. Should pivotal trials in controlled and natural infection demonstrate good efficacy for clinically relevant outcomes, clinicians and patients may accept smaller treatment effects in exchange for greater flexibility in the timing of administration to reflect when patients present to care in real-world use and this should be explored formally to support development of clinical management guidelines31,32.

Social science studies in dengue-affected communities are needed to systematically describe, explain, and predict patient and end-user preferences relevant to dengue treatment. Evidence on the safety, efficacy, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of dengue drug candidates must be integrated with considerations of how different groups perceive adverse effects, risk thresholds, and barriers to use, among others. Such insights can support ethically appropriate development and use of therapeutics as well as build trust in research and public health.

sec.title: Affordability and Pricing: A Fair Price Accessible to All who Require Treatment
sec.p: Access to anti-infective medicines is an essential part of universal health coverage. Developers of dengue therapeutics should commit to an access and delivery strategy which promotes availability at fair prices to enable use of dengue medicines at scale in all resource settings where they are needed. A fair price balances affordability for health systems and patients with sufficient incentives for innovation and the production of quality essential health products81. The Medicines Patent Pool aims to accelerate access to patented medicines on the WHO’s Model Lists of Essential Medicines82 (EML) as well as medicines with strong potential for future inclusion on the EML through supporting voluntary licensing and patent pooling83. Cost-effectiveness analyses incorporating the full range of resources required for procurement, delivery, administration, and monitoring would further support decision-making on affordability by funders and purchasers.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Safe and effective disease-specific dengue treatments are urgently needed, particularly for the growing populations ineligible for or less likely to be protected by licensed live-attenuated vaccines. These risk groups require better clinical characterisation and co-produced approaches to support their inclusion in research prioritisation, clinical trials, and care.

Therapeutics development must account for intersecting vulnerabilities arising from dengue’s geographic expansion, historical neglect, climate emergencies, and patterns of socio-economic disadvantage. Across key WHO target product profile domains—including indication for use, target population, safety and efficacy, dose regimen, and affordability and pricing—this analysis identifies ethical, regulatory, and implementation considerations relevant to the development, evaluation, and delivery of dengue therapeutics.

Strengthening of the healthcare and research ecosystem (Figure 1) will be essential to enable equitable access to dengue treatments for all. Although developed for dengue therapeutics, this framework may provide a model for integrating ethical, regulatory, and implementation considerations across the development and implementation of countermeasures for other emerging infectious threats to global health.

caption.title: Comparative Advantages of Monoclonal Antibodies and Small Molecules

tr.td: Safety, including at extremes of age, in pregnancy and lactation, and with other immunosuppression

Specificity confers low potential for off-target adverse effects. Generally well-tolerated at extremes of age, in pregnancy and lactation, and in individuals with immunosuppression. Theoretical risk of antibody-dependent enhancement in individuals with pre-existing flavivirus immunity mitigated by Fc-disabling mutations.
Higher potential for off-target adverse effects depending on mechanism and dose.
Highly specific. Resistance can emerge through viral escape mutations.
Less specific. Resistance thresholds vary depending on mechanism of action.
Half-life–extending mutations can prolong protection from 1 month to 3–6 months
Typically shorter half-lives, with elimination occurring over hours to days
